content: Registered nurses and other healthcare professionals are required to undergo extensive education, typically lasting three to four years or more, in nursing schools. This education culminates in a university or postgraduate degree, or an equivalent qualification. These professionals may hold titles such as registered nurse, nurse practitioner, clinical nurse specialist, advanced practice nurse, practice nurse, licensed nurse, diploma nurse, BS nurse, or nurse clinician. Their roles are classified under the International Standard Classification of Occupations (ISCO) as nursing professionals. The World Health Organization (WHO) has developed recommendations to guide task-sharing among healthcare workers, particularly in the provision of family planning services. These recommendations outline which types of healthcare workers can safely and effectively provide specific family planning methods. Many countries are expanding the types of providers authorized to offer contraceptive methods, with policies and regulations evolving to accommodate this shift. The WHO recommendations are applicable in both highand low-resource settings and emphasize the importance of task-specific training for healthcare workers before they begin offering these services. Additionally, effective mechanisms for monitoring, supervision, and referral are essential for successful task-sharing. Family planning services are typically offered by a range of healthcare providers, including lay health workers (e.g., community health workers), pharmacy workers, pharmacists, auxiliary nurses, auxiliary nurse-midwives, nurses, midwives, associate or advanced associate clinicians, non-specialist doctors, and specialist doctors. The specific family planning methods provided by these cadres of healthcare workers are determined by national policies and service delivery guidelines. These methods include informed choice counseling, combined oral contraceptives (COCs), progestin-only oral contraceptives (POPs), emergency contraceptive pills (ECPs), the Standard Days Method, the TwoDay Method, the lactational amenorrhea method (LAM), condoms (male and female), diaphragms, caps, spermicides, injectable contraceptives (e.g., DMPA, NET-EN, combined monthly injectables), implant insertion and removal, intrauterine devices (IUDs), vasectomy (male sterilization), and tubal ligation (female sterilization). The WHO recommendations are inclusive and do not prioritize or exclude any specific type of provider. The choice of healthcare worker for a particular task depends on local needs and conditions. All recommendations assume that healthcare workers will receive appropriate training for their assigned tasks. The implementation of task-sharing requires functioning systems for monitoring, supervision, and referral to ensure safety and effectiveness. In a user scenario involving a nurse named Aisha and a client named Hope, a 26-year-old woman brings her 6-week-old baby for routine immunizations. During the visit, Aisha discusses family planning options with Hope, who expresses interest in spacing her next pregnancy by more than a year. Aisha registers Hope in the electronic system, gathers her contact information, and provides her with a unique ID number. Hope, who is breastfeeding and has no significant health concerns, decides to start with progestin-only pills (POPs) and monitor their effects, with the possibility of switching to injectable contraceptives in the future. Aisha prescribes a one-month supply of POPs, promotes dual protection, and schedules a follow-up appointment to review Hope’s choice and provide additional supplies if needed. Aisha reassures Hope about the confidentiality of her information and offers the option of receiving appointment reminders via SMS. In another scenario, an adolescent girl visits a clinic accompanied by someone. Zeinab, a female registration clerk trained in adolescent-friendly health services, ensures the client’s privacy by moving her away from the crowded waiting area.
